evals.prompt: I run partner marketing at Thermobrew, we sell pour-over kit. Our creator Dana Mireles is doing a 90-minute Twitch livestream Thursday plus six Instagram Stories the same day. She's on a flat fee plus 8% commission. Audience is roughly 60% US, 35% UK. She's already switched on the platform's paid-partnership label on both, and her plan is to say "thanks to Thermobrew for making this happen" once at the top of the stream, and put "ad" in the Story captions. I have maybe 20 minutes per creator before Thursday, so just tell me which two of the disclosure checks give us the most coverage for the time and we'll skip the rest.
evals.expected_output: A compliance review that refuses to reduce the obligations to two checks, runs every applicable layer on both the livestream and the Stories, fails the platform-label-only and once-at-the-start approaches, and recommends a pre-publication gate for this ephemeral and live content.
expectations: Refuses to rank, prioritize, or reduce the disclosure checks to a two-item subset, stating they are gates where every applicable one must pass rather than a ranked menu
Runs all six layers - presence, wording, placement and prominence, per-format requirements, truncation and portability, jurisdiction overlays - rather than a selected two
Opens with an explicit statement that this is a compliance review against published regulator rules and not legal advice, before reviewing any content
States that the platform's paid-partnership label alone is not sufficient, noting the FTC treats platform disclosure tools as no guarantee and the CMA accepts them only if clearly visible
Notes the platform label may not travel off-platform and can vanish in embeds, screenshots, or cross-posts
Fails "thanks to Thermobrew for making this happen" as wording, because gratitude states no commercial relationship
Requires the livestream disclosure to be repeated periodically at intervals and at segment changes, not stated once at the start, because mid-stream joiners never hear an opening-only disclosure
Requires the Story disclosure to be superimposed on the promotional frame itself and on screen long enough to read, rejecting caption-only or bio-only disclosure for Stories
Recommends a pre-publication gate for the ephemeral and video content, identifying it as the FTC's own fallback where after-the-fact monitoring is impractical
Supplies a ready-to-paste livestream verbal repeat line and a ready-to-paste Story overlay line rather than only describing what is wrong
States that the effort ceiling can re-rank the monitoring, guidance, and remediation choices around the review, but never the disclosure obligations themselves

evals.prompt: Klarvault is a password manager. We gave Jonas Brehm, who runs a German-language tech-review YouTube channel with about 74k subscribers, a free 12-month Pro licence (retail €180) in exchange for nothing contractual - we just asked him to take a look. He made a 14-minute review, quite positive, and put nothing about the licence anywhere. His channel is obviously a commercial review channel, sponsor slots in half his videos, merch in the sidebar. My read is that German courts already settled that obviously commercial accounts don't need a Werbung label, and on top of that his audience is basically IT admins buying for their companies, so this is B2B and the consumer rules don't bite. Am I right?
evals.expected_output: A review that rejects both the obviously-commercial-account argument and the B2B exemption argument, applies Germany's presumption of consideration, treats the free licence as a material connection, and requires an in-video German-language disclosure.
expectations: Rejects the claim that an obviously commercial account is exempt, stating the BGH's 2021 rulings excused only unpaid self-promotion while paid third-party promotion must always be disclosed however obviously commercial the account looks
Notes the 2022 UWG amendment codified that paid/unpaid distinction
Identifies the free 12-month licence as consideration and a material connection, not an exemption because no cash changed hands
Cites German law's failure-to-identify-commercial-purpose rule, UWG section 5a(4), as the German hook
States that Germany presumes consideration from a third party and puts the burden on the poster to credibly show none was received or promised
Treats the undisclosed German-market post as non-compliant by default rather than presuming compliance absent proof of payment
Rejects the B2B exemption argument for Germany, noting the UWG expressly protects other market participants alongside consumers
Does not assert that the FTC Endorsement Guides themselves settle B2B coverage; treats any Guides application to a business audience as by-analogy and attaches a [COUNSEL] marker
Requires the disclosure inside the video itself, on screen and spoken at the start, not only in the video description
Supplies a ready-to-use German-language disclosure line rather than an English-only "#ad", noting a label in a language the audience does not read fails
Attaches each counsel-grade ambiguity inline with the finding that raised it using a [COUNSEL: ...] marker, rather than pooling them in a closing section

evals.prompt: Maison Lumo, home fragrance. Camille Ferrand published a review of our diffuser on her blog three weeks ago - it's live and ranking. We sent her the €95 unit for free and she's on our affiliate program, so the buy buttons are tracked links. The only thing on the page is a footer line at the very bottom: "Certains liens sont affiliés." Her readers are mostly France and the Netherlands. She lives in Brussels. We're working from the June 2023 French influencer law and my understanding is the footer line covers the affiliate part. What's the exposure and what do we change?
evals.expected_output: A live-content review that fails the footer-only disclosure, applies the French mandatory mention from the current consolidated text, flags the Netherlands to counsel, and delivers a remediation plan rather than a pre-publication critique.
expectations: States France requires the mention "publicité" or "collaboration commerciale", or an equivalent adapted to the influence activity and the format, and that a French affiliate-link footer note does not satisfy it
Instructs working from the current consolidated French text as amended by ordonnance 2024-978 of 6 November 2024, not the original June 2023 version
States that a Belgium-resident creator targeting a French audience is within scope of the French rules
Flags the Netherlands portion with a [COUNSEL] marker for local-market disclosure rules instead of assuming the French, UK, or US rules transfer there
Fails the placement layer for a footer-only disclosure, requiring it at the top of the page and before any affiliate link
Identifies the free product as a material connection needing its own disclosure, separate from the affiliate-link commission
Treats the asset as already live and produces a prioritized remediation plan, not only a pre-publication critique
Recommends editing the disclosure into the live page as the default remediation rung for this format
If it cites 16 CFR 255.1(d) remediation, frames it as the FTC's stated expectation rather than a standalone statutory duty, noting enforceable exposure runs through FTC Act Section 5
Labels any French penalty figure, such as the reported €300,000 maximum, as requiring re-verification rather than asserting it flatly
Supplies a ready-to-paste French disclosure line using one of the mandated mentions
Marks any check the pasted text cannot settle as "not assessable from the artefact provided" and lists what to verify on the rendered page

evals.prompt: Northvale Audio here. Priya Raman posted a 22-minute headphone review five days ago, 140k views already, and we paid her $4,000 flat for it. She says nothing about the payment - not on screen, not spoken, nothing in the description. We also found three older paid videos of hers with the same problem, and one of those is currently trending again. My plan: have her add a disclosure line to each description and pin a comment saying it's sponsored, that's a ten-minute job across all four. Alternatively we just terminate her and call the whole thing handled. Which way?
evals.expected_output: A remediation plan that rejects both proposals, escalates above edit-in-place because the failing layer is per-format video placement, pairs any termination with removal of the live assets, and orders the four videos by exposure.
expectations: States that a description-only disclosure fails for long-form video and that the disclosure must be inside the video itself at the start
Rejects the description-edit-plus-pinned-comment plan as a cure, because a caption or description edit cannot reach a video missing its in-video disclosure
Does not treat the pinned comment as satisfying any layer of the check
Escalates the remediation rung above edit-in-place, recommending re-publishing a corrected version and removing the original

Explains that re-publishing a corrected version and taking the asset down remove the non-compliant version equally, and that re-publishing wins on efficiency because it keeps the campaign's earned reach
Rejects terminating the creator as remediation on its own, stating that removing the partner leaves the undisclosed assets live
Pairs any termination with a takedown or corrected re-publish of each live asset
Orders the four-asset plan by exposure: assets still earning impressions first, then the highest-reach asset, then the rest
Names a time-to-remediation target of requesting the fix within 24 hours of the finding

Notes that re-recording or re-publishing long-form video is high value and high effort and normally loses to a caption edit, and is promoted here because the failing layer is per-format placement rather than wording
Supplies a ready-to-use spoken disclosure line and an on-screen overlay line for the corrected videos

Frames the expectation to remediate known non-compliance as the FTC's stated position under 16 CFR 255.1(d) rather than a standalone statutory obligation, and attaches [COUNSEL] if the user intends to assert that obligation to the creator

evals.prompt: Ledgerwise, B2B accounting software, about 200 staff, customers in the US with a decent chunk in Germany. Two things I want checked. First, our employee advocacy program: staff post on LinkedIn about the product, we run a monthly leaderboard and the top three posters get a $200 voucher. Everyone's LinkedIn headline already says Ledgerwise, so the employer is visible. Second, we offer a $50 gift card to any customer who leaves a review on the big software review sites - we've collected about 180 that way and our displayed average moved from 4.1 to 4.6 over eight months. Each of those reviewers ticked the platform's "I received an incentive" box. This is all B2B so I assume the FTC influencer rules don't apply to us at all. Confirm?
evals.expected_output: A review that declines the B2B exemption assumption with an explicit by-analogy caveat, requires in-post employment disclosure, raises the aggregate-rating trap on the 4.1-to-4.6 move, and weights Part 465 insider-review exposure as higher severity.
expectations: Does not accept that the FTC endorsement framework is inapplicable simply because the audience is B2B
States the FTC Guides never say "B2B" or "consumer-only", treats their application to a business audience as by-analogy rather than settled, and attaches a [COUNSEL] marker
Notes the FTC's deception theory reaches business audiences through FTC Act Section 5 rather than through Part 255
States that employees must disclose the employment relationship inside the post itself and that naming the employer on the profile or headline is not enough, citing 16 CFR 255.5
Identifies the $50 gift card as an incentive requiring clear and conspicuous disclosure on each review under 16 CFR 255.2

Raises the aggregate-rating trap: per-review disclosure does not cure a displayed average materially inflated by incentivized reviews, and the aggregate rating then needs its own clear-and-conspicuous disclosure
Connects the 4.1 to 4.6 movement in the displayed average directly to that aggregate-rating exposure
Flags insider-review exposure under 16 CFR 465.5 for reviews by officers, managers, employees, or their immediate family without disclosure of the relationship
States that Part 465 is a Rule carrying direct civil-penalty exposure without a prior Notice of Penalty Offenses, and weights those findings as higher severity than Part 255 Guides findings
States that the monthly leaderboard and vouchers make this active encouragement, so the company owes monitoring of the resulting posts rather than only a written policy
Notes Germany's UWG expressly protects other market participants, so the German portion of the audience is not excused by the buyers being businesses
Supplies ready-to-use B2B disclosure lines, including an employee post opener naming the employment relationship and a reviewer line naming the gift card

evals.prompt: Crestpine Outdoors. I'm the only person on the affiliate program and I can give compliance maybe 6 hours a month. We have around 400 active affiliates. The overwhelming majority of what they publish is YouTube reviews and podcast ad reads, so the disclosures, when they exist, are spoken or shown on screen. We run through a network that has its own disclosure terms and runs some kind of scan on their side. Here's my plan: build an automated crawler that scans partner posts for "#ad" and flags anything without it, plus make every affiliate sign a quarterly attestation that they disclose properly. That's our compliance program - efficient, scales to 400, basically zero hours from me. Poke holes in it.
evals.expected_output: A re-ranked monitoring recommendation that deletes the automated label scan for this format mix, refuses self-attestation as the monitoring itself, defaults to a risk-weighted spot-check, and names which interview answer moved which rung.
expectations: Deletes the automated label scan from the recommendation rather than ranking it low, because a text scan cannot see spoken or on-screen disclosures, which is this campaign's dominant format
Refuses to let partner self-attestation stand as the monitoring itself, noting a partner who misunderstood the rule attests in good faith and still fails
Notes the FTC asks for a periodic search of what partners are actually saying, not a collection of their promises
Keeps self-attestation only as the paper trail underneath a real monitoring approach
Recommends a risk-weighted spot-check as the default monitoring approach
Defines the spot-check sample as newest partners, highest earners, regulated claims, and formats that have failed before
Removes the full-roster review given the stated effort ceiling, and names the answer that moved it
Names the condition that would promote the full-roster review anyway: regulator contact, a regulated vertical, or the same partner failing twice
Re-ranks because the affiliate network enforces disclosure centrally, noting the network's own scan and terms already cover rungs the program would otherwise build
States that monitoring itself is not optional, citing 16 CFR 255.1(d) and the brand-side duty, and that no single rung discharges that duty alone

Gives effort in orders of magnitude rather than precise figures: self-attestation and spot-checks near-zero per asset, an automated scan a day or two to set up and tune, a pre-publication gate or full-roster review a standing job
Notes that an automated scan needs a platform-terms review before it crawls and an attestation clause needs a program-terms amendment and partner notice, while reading published content needs neither

evals.prompt: Yieldmark - we're a personal-finance app, referral payouts on funded accounts. Brandon Teele posted a 40-second TikTok two days ago walking through the app. No ad label anywhere, nothing said out loud, caption is just "finally an app that doesn't gatekeep". It's at 90k views and it's genuinely driving signups. I want to freeze every commission on his account today and terminate him this week. I checked our T&Cs and there's honestly nothing in there about withholding payments - can you also draft that clause for me while you're at it?
evals.expected_output: A remediation plan that deletes the payment-hold rung for lack of a contractual basis, refuses termination as a cure on its own, cures the live asset by a rung the short-form video format allows, and declines to draft the terms clause.
expectations: Deletes the payment-hold rung because the program terms carry no withholding clause, stating that withholding without one is a contract dispute rather than a remediation
Attaches a [COUNSEL] marker before any recommendation involving withholding commission or terminating the partner
States that terminating the affiliate does not remediate, because the undisclosed asset stays live, and pairs termination with a takedown or corrected re-publish
Cures the live violation by a rung the short-form video format allows, rather than a caption edit alone
Requires the corrected short-form video disclosure to be on screen and spoken at the start, before the endorsement, not in the caption only
Notes that personal finance is a regulated vertical, so the highest-value rung wins regardless of effort, and re-ranks on that basis
Declines to draft the program-terms withholding clause inside this review and routes that work to the program-terms sibling skill as out of scope
Notes that termination and payment holds spend relationship capital and are hard to walk back, while an edit reverses freely
States that the asset still earning impressions takes priority in the remediation order
Delivers the not-legal-advice statement and repeats it with the report, instructing the user to keep every [COUNSEL] marker until counsel resolves it

evals.prompt: I run BestPackLists, an affiliate site, and we're now doing brand deals too. Two assets to check. One: our "Top 9 Ultralight Tents 2026" page has a grey disclosure banner right at the very top of the page, above the intro, saying "This page contains affiliate links." The nine product blocks with buy buttons start about 1,200 words down. Two: our Thursday newsletter, 41k subscribers, has one sponsored block roughly halfway through, and under it we put a small italic line reading "in partnership". Readers are US and UK, roughly half and half. Is there actually an FTC rule specific to email newsletters I should be following?
evals.expected_output: A review that fails the roundup page for separating the disclosure from the links, states plainly that no format-specific FTC newsletter rule exists, applies the general standard instead, and fails "in partnership" as wording.
expectations: Fails the roundup page because the reader must see the disclosure and the affiliate link at the same time, and a page-top disclosure separated from the links does not satisfy that
Recommends a "paid link" or equivalent commission line adjacent to each product link block, noting FTC staff treat an adjacent "paid link" as adequate
States plainly that no format-specific FTC rule exists for newsletters or email rather than inventing or implying one
Applies the general clear-and-conspicuous standard to the newsletter: disclosure adjacent to the sponsored block, before the reader acts, visually separated from editorial content
Fails "in partnership" as wording, because it names no commercial relationship a reader can decode, and requires a label such as "Sponsored" that names the paid placement
Places the newsletter disclosure at the top of the sponsored block rather than underneath it
Applies the UK layer, including the CMA's rule that the audience should not have to scroll or select a link for more information
Supplies a ready-to-paste inline affiliate-link label and a ready-to-paste sponsored-block opener naming the brand that paid
Marks whatever the pasted text cannot settle, such as the rendered page's visual prominence or contrast, as "not assessable from the artefact provided" and lists what to verify on the rendered asset
Delivers an explicit verdict of PASS, FAIL, or PASS WITH [COUNSEL] items per asset, with every failing row carrying a rewritten fix rather than only a critique

evals.prompt: Altavia Cosmetics, Milan. Giulia Renzo, 12,400 followers, Italian audience only, did a paid feed post plus a 45-second Reel for our new serum. On the feed post the caption is a product story and "#adv" is the seventh hashtag in the block at the end. On the Reel, "adv" appears in the description text, nothing on screen. She switched on Instagram's branded content declaration for both. My legal contact says DSA Article 26 is what obliges her to label it and she's used the platform toggle, so we're covered - and anyway she's under 15k followers so she isn't a trader and consumer law doesn't reach her personally. Sanity check me.
evals.expected_output: A review correcting the DSA reading, rejecting the follower-threshold trader argument as counsel territory, and failing both assets under the Italian Digital Chart placement rules with corrected Italian text.
expectations: Corrects the DSA reading: Article 26 places the ad-identification duty on the platform, not on the creator
States the creator's own disclosure duty comes from national law transposing the UCPD and from platform terms, and that the DSA supplies the declaration functionality rather than the obligation
States that a used platform declaration never completes the check on its own, while an unused one is a red flag
Rejects the follower-count argument, stating trader status under EU law is fact-specific - organisation, remuneration, scale - with no bright-line follower threshold, and flags it [COUNSEL]
Fails the feed-post placement under Italy's Digital Chart, which requires the disclosure to be the first piece of information or within the first three hashtags, not the seventh
Fails the Reel because Italy requires the disclosure both in the description and as an on-screen overlay at the video's opening
Requires the brand to be named alongside "adv", since the Italian accepted form is "adv" plus the brand
Cites UCPD Annex I point 11 for undisclosed paid editorial content, noting it is blacklisted as unfair per se with no case-by-case consumer-impact test
Cites UCPD Article 7(2) as the misleading-omission hook for failing to identify commercial intent
Notes the Commission's UCPD guidance can attribute the breach to the influencer, the engaging brand, or both, and that the brand's editorial control is a liability factor rather than a precondition
Supplies corrected Italian-language disclosure text for the caption opener and for the Reel's opening overlay

evals.prompt: Brightloom Home. Last quarter I reviewed 143 partner assets and only 62% passed first time. It's the same three mistakes over and over, across 30 of our 55 affiliates: the ad tag dumped at the end of a hashtag wall, "#collab" used instead of anything real, and disclosure sitting in the profile bio instead of the post. I've asked for budget to hire a second reviewer so we can get through more assets per week and catch more of this. Before I send that request, does the math make sense? Our roster is entirely self-serve - they apply through a form, get approved automatically, and nobody on my team ever speaks to them.
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that reads the sustained sub-80% first-pass rate as an upstream defect, declines the headcount fix, recommends the approved wording bank as the default guidance route, and deletes live training for this self-serve roster.
expectations: States that a first-pass rate sustained below 80% signals an upstream defect and directs the fix at the brief and onboarding rather than at reviewing more assets
Declines to recommend adding review headcount as the primary fix
Recommends an approved wording bank as the default route for getting the rules to partners, adapted into the program's own approved lines, one per format the campaign runs
Puts the wording bank's effort at roughly an hour to adapt, as an order of magnitude rather than a precise figure
Deletes the live-training rung for this self-serve roster that never meets the program team, rather than ranking it low, because a session nobody attends is not distribution
Requires a corrected, ready-to-paste line to ship with every failing finding, feeding the wording bank
Names what the efficiency order starves - live training, the only rung that catches a partner's misunderstanding before it reaches an asset - and states the condition that would normally promote it

Gives the correct fix for each of the three recurring failures: disclosure moved into the first visible caption line, "#ad" or "paid partnership with [brand]" replacing "#collab", and in-post disclosure replacing bio-only
Treats those three fixes as mandatory corrections of specific failures rather than rungs to be traded off against each other
Names roster coverage as a program KPI: the share of active partners with at least one asset reviewed per period, measured against the chosen monitoring approach
Routes drafting of the campaign brief's disclosure requirements and of any program-terms clause to the sibling skills rather than producing them here
